subsystems.name: Microporous core
subsystems.role: holds the panel apart under atmospheric pressure while conducting as little heat as possible.
parts: fumed silica or needled glass-fibre mat
opacifier particles (e.g. silicon carbide, carbon black) that block radiant heat

subsystems.name: Barrier envelope
subsystems.role: keeps air out for the panel's whole life; even a slow leak ruins performance.
parts: multilayer film of metallised polymer and aluminium layers

subsystems.name: Sealed edge
subsystems.role: the welded seam that closes the envelope after evacuation.

subsystems.name: Getter and desiccant
subsystems.role: mops up residual gas and moisture that outgas from the core over years.

subsystems.name: Panel assembly
subsystems.role: turns a fragile vacuum bag into a buildable product.

subsystems.name: Quality control
subsystems.role: confirms each panel actually holds its vacuum.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the core
buildSteps.detail: Fumed silica is mixed with an opacifier and pressed into boards, or glass fibre is needled into a mat. Pore sizes of tens of nanometres to a few micrometres are what let the core support atmospheric load and keep gas conduction low.

buildSteps.title: Dry the core
buildSteps.detail: Residual moisture would raise internal pressure, so the core is baked or dried before bagging.

buildSteps.title: Bag it
buildSteps.detail: The core, plus a getter pouch, is placed inside the multilayer barrier film and partly sealed.

buildSteps.title: Evacuate
buildSteps.detail: The bag goes into a vacuum chamber and is pumped down to a small fraction of atmospheric pressure — a few millibar or less. Fumed-silica cores tolerate more residual gas than glass-fibre cores.

buildSteps.title: Seal under vacuum
buildSteps.detail: Still inside the chamber, the final seam is heat-sealed, trapping the vacuum inside the film.

buildSteps.title: Test every panel
buildSteps.detail: Thermal conductivity is measured; a panel that reads too high is rejected before it leaves the factory.

buildSteps.title: Assemble into building elements
buildSteps.detail: Panels are framed into wall, roof or floor cassettes with foam or sealant around the edges, because the film itself conducts heat and creates a thermal bridge.

buildSteps.title: Install without cutting
buildSteps.detail: VIPs cannot be trimmed on site; each is made to the exact size and must be protected from screws, nails and abrasion. Typical thermal conductivity is about 0.004–0.008 W/(m·K), against roughly 0.035–0.040 for mineral wool.

prerequisites.why: without a film that blocks air and water vapour for decades, the vacuum is lost and the panel becomes ordinary insulation.

prerequisites.tech: Fumed silica and microporous core materials
prerequisites.why: the core must resist atmospheric pressure — around 10 tonnes per square metre — without collapsing.
panels must be evacuated and sealed in one continuous process.
small amounts of gas and water vapour slowly appear inside any sealed panel and must be absorbed.
building designers need reliable 25–50 year performance figures, and test methods for this are still maturing.

pathway.milestone: VIPs in refrigerators, freezers and temperature-controlled shipping containers, plus niche building retrofits where wall thickness is limited
pathway.unlocks: high insulation in spaces where conventional thickness will not fit.

pathway.milestone: factory-made wall and roof cassettes with VIPs already framed in
pathway.unlocks: removes on-site puncture risk, which is the main cause of failure today.

pathway.milestone: improved barrier films and core formulations that hold vacuum longer at lower cost
pathway.unlocks: wider use in ordinary buildings rather than only specialist niches.

pathway.milestone: whole-building envelopes combining VIPs with aerogels and phase-change layers, with recyclable cores
pathway.unlocks: very low heating demand in existing buildings without thick added walls.
